Title: Vera Molnár
BodyText: Vera Molnár was a Hungarian media artist who lived and worked in France. Molnár is widely considered to have been a pioneer of computer art and generative art and was also one of the first women to use computers in her art practice.

Title: Lauren Lee McCarthy
BodyText:
Lauren Lee McCarthy is an artist examining social relationships in the midst of automation, surveillance, and algorithmic living. She has received grants and residencies from Creative Capital, United States Artists, LACMA, Sundance, Eyebeam, Pioneer Works, Autodesk, and Ars Electronica, and her work is in the collection of the Whitney Museum of American Art. Her work SOMEONE was awarded the Ars Electronica Golden Nica and the Japan Media Arts Social Impact Award, and her work LAUREN was awarded the IDFA DocLab Award for Immersive Non-Fiction. . Lauren is also the creator of p5.js, an open-source art and education platform that prioritizes access and diversity in learning to code, with over 10 million users. She expanded on this work in her role from 2015–21 on the Board of Directors for the Processing Foundation, whose mission is to serve those who have historically not had access to the fields of technology, code, and art in learning software and visual literacy. Lauren is a Professor at UCLA Design Media Arts. She holds an MFA from UCLA and a BS Computer Science and BS Art and Design from MIT.

"I am working with performance, software, electronics, internet, film, photography, installation. My work exists within and beyond the gallery, seeking edges of art and media performance. There are different layers of experience, from the intimate performance to a much wider audience invited in through the ripples of viral videos and media coverage.Each work feels like an attempt to hack my way out of myself and into closeness with others. I am embodying machines, trying to understand that distance between the algorithm and myself, the distance between others and me. Title: Code Poetry delta_t.bf
BodyText: delta t is a series of interactive sketches by Code/Poetry that explore the sonification of temporal data. It turns system time into generative sound patterns through interfaces that visually mimic modular synth patches. This work feels particularly relevant to the creative coding module, as it demonstrates how data, sound, and interface design intersect poetically. The clean, abstract interface and the conceptual transparency of the patching metaphor deeply influenced the way I think about interaction in code.

Title: my little piece of privacy
BodyText: Niklas Roy’s kinetic sculpture My Little Piece of Privacy features a robotic curtain that uses computer vision to block out the gaze of passersby. Installed in a street-facing window, it humorously inverts surveillance by making the curtain ‘watch’ others. It relates to the physical computing module through its real-time environmental responsiveness. The piece also reflects on themes of agency, privacy, and absurdity in tech—offering critical commentary through playful engineering. This inspired my approach to humorous and reactive design in interactive environments.
